Neonatal Tokay geckos emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a snout–vent length of approximately 4.8 cm [Lb = approximately 4.8 cm], a size that facilitates early climbing and escape from terrestrial predators. Hatchlings weigh just 2.4 grams [Wwb = 2.4 grams] upon emergence, reflecting the energetic constraints of yolk provisioning within a cleidoic egg. These diminutive dimensions contrast sharply with the adult body plan, as females ultimately attain a maximum wet weight of 150.7 grams [Wwi = 150.7 grams] after several years of sustained growth. The progression from a 2.4 grams neonate to a 150.7 grams adult requires a lengthy period of somatic development, during which the gecko must navigate the thermal heterogeneity of its tropical habitat. Field measurements indicate that this growth trajectory is strongly modulated by ambient temperature; in captive colonies maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], individuals reach sexual maturity only after a prolonged juvenile phase characterized by steady but gradual increases in both length and mass.

Female Tokay geckos undergo puberty when their snout–vent length reaches about 17.3 cm [Lp = about 17.3 cm], a threshold that signals the onset of gonadal activation and the capacity for vitellogenesis. This pubertal size is considerably smaller than the ultimate female SVL of 20.9 cm [Li = 20.9 cm], indicating that several more months of growth separate first reproductive competence from asymptotic body size. The relationship between size at puberty and maximum size aligns with patterns observed in other large-bodied gekkonids, where females allocate substantial resources to continued linear expansion even after initiating reproductive activity. Attaining 17.3 cm typically requires between twelve and eighteen months under favorable thermal regimes, after which females begin to produce clutches of parchment-shelled eggs at regular intervals. Asymptotic size in females is reached at 20.9 cm [Li = 20.9 cm], after which somatic growth in snout–vent length virtually ceases, though body mass may continue to vary with reproductive status and lipid storage.

Reproductive output in Gekko gecko follows a pattern of iteroparous egg production typical of many tropical geckos. Under thermal conditions maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a gravid female deposits one to two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one to two eggs per clutch], with individuals capable of producing approximately 10 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 10 clutches each year]. This high frequency of oviposition yields a maximum annual reproductive rate that reflects the species' ability to exploit warm temperatures throughout much of the year. The parchment-shelled eggs are typically glued to sheltered substrates such as tree hollows or rocky crevices, where they undergo incubation for roughly two to three months depending on local thermal conditions. At the constant temperature of 27 °C, the interval between successive clutches can be as short as one month, allowing a single female to produce up to fifteen eggs annually under optimal resource availability. This fecundity is modest compared to some small-bodied lizards, but the combination of large egg size and frequent oviposition represents a successful strategy for a long-lived, slow-maturing predator.

Longevity records for wild Tokay geckos are scarce, but captive data suggest that individuals maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C] can live for approximately 23.5 years [am = approximately 23.5 years], a remarkably long lifespan for a lizard of this body size. This extended reproductive window compensates for the relatively low annual fecundity, allowing females to accumulate substantial lifetime reproductive output despite producing only one or two eggs per clutch. The capacity for reproductive senescence appears limited in this species, with captive females retaining the ability to produce viable clutches well into their second decade of life. At 27 °C, maximum documented longevity approaches 8,578 days [am = approaches 8,578 days] in carefully monitored laboratory colonies, though wild individuals likely experience reduced survivorship due to predation and resource limitation at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Comparative analyses indicate that this lifespan far exceeds that of most similarly sized geckos, reflecting the Tokay's large body size, low metabolic rate, and adaptation to stable tropical environments where seasonal mortality pressures are moderate.

Adult female Tokay geckos attain a maximum snout–vent length of 20.9 cm [Li = 20.9 cm], which corresponds to a total length of approximately 40 cm when including the robust tail — a dimension that facilitates both arboreal locomotion and intraspecific combat among territorial males. This substantial body size places Gekko gecko among the largest extant gekkonids, a status that carries important ecological implications for thermoregulation, territorial defense, and prey handling. The wet weight of 150.7 grams [Wwi = 150.7 grams] in reproductively active females represents a significant energetic investment, with gravid individuals carrying the additional mass of two large, yolk-laden eggs within the oviducts. Comparisons with the SVL at puberty of about 17.3 cm [Lp = about 17.3 cm] reveal that females continue to add nearly 3.6 cm of snout–vent length after initiating reproduction, a pattern that allows for increasing clutch volume with age. The ontogenetic transformation from a 4.8 cm [Lb = 4.8 cm] neonatal SVL to a 20.9 cm [Li = 20.9 cm] adult SVL is well documented through mark-recapture studies in Southeast Asian populations, where stable thermal conditions support rapid juvenile growth before the deceleration characteristic of asymptotic size.
